summary: This informational RFC lists frequently asked questions from IETF meeting attendees about travel logistics and local information. It helps people who offer local advice prepare answers, for example on the IETF wiki or a meeting site.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a trip to a new town, people ask what to bring and where to eat. This lists the questions so hosts can prepare answers.

questions: what do ietf attendees ask about travel
where to find ietf meeting travel information
what should ietf hosts tell attendees
how do i plan a trip to an ietf meeting
subtitle: A guidebook for meeting hosts to help travelers find local information

tldr.problem: IETF attendees come from 50+ countries and ask the same travel questions at every meeting, overwhelming local staff and wasting time as each person searches separately online.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a complete list of frequently asked question categories (travel, health, food, communications, weather, fitness) so that local hosts can pre-populate answers in a wiki or website before the meeting.
tldr.outcome: Attendees find reliable local information quickly, organizers reduce repetitive inquiries, and hosts understand what attendees need without rediscovering the list at each meeting.

today: RFC 6640 is Informational and serves as a reference for IETF meeting hosts. The IETF wiki and host websites continue to use this list as a template for organizing local information. No updates have obsoleted it.

sections.title: Why IETF Attendees Need Local Information
sections.content:
The IETF holds meetings in cities around the world, and attendees arrive from over 50 countries. Most have never been to the location before. They need practical information: how to get from the airport to their hotel, where to eat lunch during the conference, how to pay for a taxi, whether the water is safe to drink, and where to find a gym.

Meeting organizers and volunteers who speak the local language are ideal sources for this information, but they receive the same questions from hundreds of people in the days before the meeting, which overwhelms them. This RFC exists so organizers know what questions to expect and can prepare answers in advance on a wiki or website, turning a flood of emails into a single published resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of travelers come to IETF meetings in strange cities. They ask the same questions hundreds of times. This document says what to answer before they ask.

sections.title: Travel Logistics
sections.content:
Attendees need to know which airports and train stations serve the city, how long it takes to reach their hotel, and how much a taxi costs. They should also understand local transit: which buses or trains to take, how to buy a ticket, and where stations are located. For those unfamiliar with the area, even reading a sign in a foreign script can be difficult, so maps in English, instructions on how to use the transit system, and even pictures of station logos help.

Information about whether to use a taxi, rent a car, or use public transit varies widely by city. In some places, a rental car is essential; in others, driving is impractical and mass transit is the only option. Whether the conference venue is walking distance from hotels, or requires a shuttle, also matters significantly to attendees planning their time.
sections.plainLanguage: How do I get from the plane to my hotel? How much will it cost? Can I take a bus? Can I read the signs? This section answers those.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
Travelers need to know about electrical outlets and voltage (so they know whether their devices will work), visa requirements, languages spoken, and holidays or strikes that might affect the meeting. Health and safety information is vital: phone numbers for emergency services, locations of hospitals, neighborhoods to avoid, and whether the local water is drinkable. Information about air quality, smoking rules indoors, and the temperature indoors (which varies dramatically between climates and buildings) helps people prepare.

Payment methods matter greatly: which credit cards are accepted, where ATMs are located, tipping customs, and currency exchange rates. Some cities have local scams or unusual taxi practices that travelers should know about. For people with dietary restrictions, information about vegetarian, vegan, halal, and kosher options, and how to communicate these needs to restaurant staff, is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: Will my phone charger work? Is it safe? Can I get money? Can I eat what I eat at home? What do I say about it in the local language? This section covers daily survival.

sections.title: Food, Fitness, and Enjoyment
sections.content:
Food deserves special attention because the IETF's schedule sends about 1000 people to restaurants at once during the lunch break. Information about nearby restaurants organized by price, type of cuisine, and distance from the venue helps attendees make plans. Details about which restaurants need reservations, whether they have rush times to avoid, and whether they offer quick options for working lunches all prove useful.

Some attendees exercise during the conference. Information about running paths, gyms, soccer fields (for the informal "soccer BoF"), and swimming facilities helps them stay active. Finally, many attendees add a day or two for sightseeing before or after the meeting. Links to tourist attractions, local events, and information about souvenirs and locally crafted items complete the picture, turning a work trip into an opportunity to experience a new city.
sections.plainLanguage: Where can I eat? Can I grab lunch fast? Where can I run? What should I see while I'm here? Nice-to-have information for a better trip.
